chief_complaint: severe back pain, fatigue, and frequent infections
hpi_details: 68F presents with 3 months of worsening lower back pain, profound fatigue, and two episodes of pneumonia requiring antibiotics. Labs show a new normocytic anemia, elevated creatinine, and hypercalcemia.

core_concepts: CRAB criteria: Calcium elevation, Renal insufficiency, Anemia, Bone lesions.
common_misconceptions: Attributing back pain in elderly solely to osteoarthritis when there are systemic red flags.
dangerous_errors: Missing impending spinal cord compression from a vertebral body lesion.
management_principles: SPEP/UPEP, skeletal survey, bone marrow biopsy, oncology referral.
boundaries_and_exceptions: Specific drug dosages, monitoring protocols, and referral criteria must be tailored to organ function, comorbidities, and local hospital pathways.
Atypical presentations in elderly, pediatric, or immunocompromised patients may require lower thresholds for inpatient monitoring and specialist consultation.

source_refs.title: UpToDate & National Evidence-Based Clinical Practice Guidelines 2026

reference_soap.subjective: 68F with chronic severe back pain, recurrent infections, and fatigue.
reference_soap.objective: Pale conjunctiva, midline lumbar spine tenderness. Labs show Ca 11.2, Cr 1.8, Hgb 9.5.
reference_soap.plan: SPEP with immunofixation, skeletal survey, nephrology and hematology consults.

learning_objectives: Identify the CRAB criteria for multiple myeloma.

teaching.one_liner: An elderly patient with bone pain, anemia, renal dysfunction, and hypercalcemia (CRAB criteria).
red_flags: New bone pain in elderly with anemia/hypercalcemia

must_ask.say: Where exactly is the back pain, and has it been getting worse over the past months?
Have you been getting infections more often than usual recently?
Have you noticed less urine output, or symptoms of feeling thirsty or confused?
Have you had any weakness in your legs, numbness, or trouble controlling your bladder or bowels?
How is the fatigue affecting your usual daily activities?

history.answer: I've been suffering from terrible lower back pain for the past three months, and lately I feel completely exhausted all the time.
The pain is located right in the center of my lower back. It stays right there and does not radiate down into my legs or feet.
It crept up on me gradually about three months ago. There was no heavy lifting, fall, or accident that triggered it.
It is a constant, deep, gnawing ache in the bone that feels like a seven out of ten in severity.
Walking, standing, or bending over worsens the ache significantly. Sitting still helps slightly, but it never completely fades away.
Yes, lying flat in bed does not ease the pain, and it frequently wakes me up in the middle of the night.
I feel a little stiff when I first get out of bed for maybe ten minutes, but moving around does not improve the pain at all.
No, I haven't noticed any numbness, tingling, or weakness in my legs or feet.
No, I have normal bladder and bowel control, and I have normal feeling around my groin and private area.
My back aches when I walk, but my calves do not cramp up or go numb, and leaning forward doesn't relieve it like a shopping cart would.
I do not have a fever or chills right now, and I haven't had drenching night sweats.
I haven't had much of an appetite, and I have lost about four kilograms over the past two months without trying.
I have been experiencing overwhelming fatigue every single day. Even getting dressed or doing light chores leaves me completely worn out.
I came down with pneumonia twice over the last four months and needed antibiotics each time, which has never happened to me before.
I have felt unusually thirsty and noticed I'm urinating more frequently, along with feeling mildly nauseated and constipated recently.
No, I have no stomach pain, no pulsing sensation in my belly, and no burning or blood in my urine.
No eye redness or pain, no pain in my heels, no persistent diarrhea, and no skin rashes or psoriasis.
I have never had any kind of cancer, and my past routine cancer screenings were all normal.
I was told I had mild osteopenia a few years ago, but I have never had a bone fracture and have never taken steroid pills.
No, I have never had acupuncture, epidural injections, nerve blocks, or back operations.
I tried taking acetaminophen and over-the-counter ibuprofen regularly, but they barely touched the pain.
I initially thought I just strained a muscle while gardening, but because it keeps getting worse, I'm really not sure what's going on.
I noticed my urine looked slightly foamy and I've been feeling so thirsty, so I'm worried that my kidneys might be failing.
I really want to find out what is causing this deep back pain and get something to treat it so I can sleep again.
I have had high blood pressure for about eight years. I don't have diabetes, heart disease, or kidney problems that I knew of.
I had my appendix removed when I was twenty-five, but no other surgeries and no hospital stays until those recent pneumonia clinic visits.
I take amlodipine five milligrams once daily for my high blood pressure, and occasional acetaminophen for my back.
I have no known allergies to any medicines, foods, or latex.
I have never smoked cigarettes or used any tobacco products.
I drink half a glass of red wine once or twice a year on holidays, practically none.
I am a retired elementary school teacher and live at home with my husband.
My mother had high blood pressure and passed away from a stroke in her eighties, and my father had heart disease. No family history of blood diseases or cancer.
I went through menopause naturally around age fifty-one and haven't had any postmenopausal spotting or bleeding.

exam.finding: Blood pressure 135/85 mmHg, pulse 78 beats/min, respiratory rate 16 breaths/min, body temperature 36.8°C, oxygen saturation 98% on room air.
Definite pallor of the palpebral conjunctivae bilaterally; sclerae are non-icteric.
Soft, non-distended, and non-tender throughout; no abdominal aortic enlargement or pulsatile mass palpable.
No costovertebral angle tenderness on percussion bilaterally.

Marked tenderness on palpation and gentle percussion over the midline lower lumbar spinous processes; active lumbar range of motion is restricted by pain; straight leg raise test is negative bilaterally.
Motor strength is 5/5 in bilateral hip flexors, quadriceps, tibialis anterior, extensor hallucis longus, and gastrocnemius muscles.
Normal and symmetric light touch and pinprick sensation throughout both lower extremities and the perianal region.
Patellar and Achilles tendon reflexes are 2+ bilaterally; Babinski sign is negative bilaterally.
Normal resting anal sphincter tone and intact voluntary squeeze; no masses or tenderness palpable.
